title: Rethinking Retrieval in the Long-Context Era: Training-Free Semantic Trees for Adaptive Context Construction

paper.title: Rethinking Retrieval in the Long-Context Era: Training-Free Semantic Trees for Adaptive Context Construction
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making
full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However,
greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not
which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking
retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing
its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts
and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile
these goals, we introduce TreeFuse , a training-free framework that uses semantic
abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. TreeFuse constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a
single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query,
structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate
shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural
relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, TreeFuse improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three
LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average
while reducing answer-context length by 58.55%. Our code is available at the code repository .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Frontier language models can increasingly accommodate entire documents within their context windows, making full-context prompting a practical option for long-document question answering. Yet input capacity and context selection address different questions: how much information a model can receive, and which information it should receive for a particular query. Prior work shows that performance can depend strongly on where relevant information appears within a long context, even when that information remains available to the model \citep liu2024lost. Prior compression methods show that selecting context can improve answering as well as shorten the input \citep longllmlingua2024,provence2025, while LaRA \citep lara2025 finds no universally preferable choice between retrieval-based and full-context approaches. These findings motivate rethinking retrieval beyond accommodating input-length constraints: When the full document already fits within the context window, can retrieval improve answering, and how should it select the supporting context? A relevant passage is not always sufficient to support an answer. A question may require a directly mentioned fact together with background or a relation established elsewhere in the document. Sufficient Context \citep joren2025sufficient explicitly distinguishes contextual support from answer correctness. Context construction must therefore consider both the support it retains and how selectively it presents that support. Narrow extraction can omit a necessary fact or separate a detail from its interpretation, whereas broad expansion may introduce unrelated material. Controlled studies of arithmetic reasoning show that such irrelevant information can interfere with model predictions \citep shi2023distracted, motivating attention to context concentration as well as support retention. Hierarchical methods such as HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 make document organization available to retrieval and refinement. The remaining design question is how to use that organization while remaining sensitive to precise source-level details. Figure 1: A schematic example contrasts full context with distractors, incomplete retrieval with missing support, and TreeFuse ’s focused context retaining both supporting statements. To reconcile support retention with context concentration, we separate the information used to select evidence from the text supplied for answering. Figure 1 illustrates the goal: retaining supporting facts and their relation while excluding unrelated material. We instantiate this principle with TreeFuse , a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while preserving original evidence. Step 1: Source-grounded Semantic Tree Construction. A pretrained model jointly proposes semantic boundaries and hierarchical relations from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to original source spans. The resulting hierarchy is query-independent and reusable. Step 2: Query-adaptive Context Construction. Structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate nodes from this shared representation. A localized lexical match can retain a complete source node, supplementing semantic judgments with precise details. The selected nodes and their ancestors form a pruned hierarchy that preserves the original parent–child relations and complete local text. The same constructed context can be supplied to different answer models without model-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate TreeFuse with four frontier answer models that offer strong long-context processing capabilities: Qwen3.8-Max \citep qwen38max2026, DeepSeek-V4-Pro \citep deepseekv4doc2026, Kimi-K2.6 \citep kimik26blog2026, and GLM-5.3 \citep glm53docs2026. Full-context prompting provides a direct reference for testing whether retrieval remains beneficial when the complete document is already available to the answer model. Across three LongBench QA tasks, TreeFuse reduces the answer-context length by 58.55% on average while improving the four-model average by 1.72 QA-F1 points over full-context prompting. The gains are more pronounced on the multi-hop HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA tasks, where the four-model averages improve by 1.72 and 2.46 points, respectively. On 2WikiMQA with Kimi-K2.6, TreeFuse achieves a 7.00-point improvement, corresponding to a 14.76% relative gain. Evaluation on LaRA further tests transfer across heterogeneous long-document tasks, where TreeFuse achieves the highest four-model average accuracy among the evaluated methods with 43.87% less answer context. Beyond answer scores, source-evidence analyses examine completeness and concentration, while component comparisons characterize semantic and lexical selection, hierarchical organization, and single-pass construction. These evaluations address both parts of our research question, establishing average gains over full-context prompting and examining how the selected contexts retain and organize supporting evidence. To summarize, our contributions are: • We empirically demonstrate that query-adaptive context construction can improve average answering performance even when full-document input is feasible, positioning retrieval as a complement to long-context capacity. • We introduce reusable semantic trees and dual-granularity selection to coordinate structural support with precise source details, retaining complete local text without method-specific training. • We provide a broad evaluation across four frontier answer-model families and diverse long-document tasks, obtaining a 1.72-point average QA-F1 improvement on the three LongBench tasks with 58.55% less context. We release our code to support research on adaptive context construction: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE .

sections.heading: Retrieval and Compression for Long-Context Question Answering
sections.text: LongBench \citep longbench2024 and LaRA \citep lara2025 evaluate long-context understanding and retrieval-based answering. LongRAG by \citet jiang2024longrag groups related documents into larger retrieval units to exploit long-context models. A separate LongRAG by \citet zhao2024longrag jointly addresses global information and factual details in long-context QA. Compression methods act at different granularities: LongLLMLingua \citep longllmlingua2024 prunes tokens, Provence \citep provence2025 selects sentences, and RECOMP \citep recomp2024 and BRIEF-Pro \citep briefpro2026 learn or generate compact contexts. ACC-RAG \citep accrag2025 adapts compression rates, while SARA \citep sara2025 combines textual and compressed representations. Sufficient Context \citep joren2025sufficient examines whether supplied information is sufficient for answering.

sections.heading: Semantic Chunking and Hierarchical Document Indexing
sections.text: Semantic chunkers such as LumberChunker \citep lumberchunker2024 and Meta-Chunking \citep metachunking2025 seek coherent boundaries, with libraries such as Chonkie 1 1 1 https://docs.chonkie.ai/ providing multiple implementations. Hierarchical indexes additionally organize relationships among units. RAPTOR \citep raptor2024 recursively clusters and summarizes passages. TreeRAG \citep tao2025treerag combines tree-based chunking with bidirectional traversal. SiReRAG \citep zhang2025sirerag constructs similarity and relatedness trees and combines their nodes in a retrieval pool. Heading-aware indexing \citep headingaware2025 exploits existing sections, while HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 learn specialized components for hierarchical chunking or refinement.

sections.heading: Structure-Aware and Hybrid Retrieval
sections.text: BM25 \citep robertson2009bm25 and DPR \citep karpukhin2020dpr provide lexical and learned semantic relevance signals. Contextual Retrieval \citep anthropic2024contextual prepends explanatory context to chunks before embedding and BM25 indexing. MemWalker \citep chen2023memwalker interactively navigates summary trees, while PageIndex \citep pageindex2025 uses reasoning-based search over document hierarchies. HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 expands retrieval hits through Auto-Merge, and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 performs query-aware refinement. DISRetrieval \citep chen2026disretrieval combines discourse parsing, LLM-enhanced node representations, and structure-guided hierarchical retrieval. TreeFuse approaches retrieval as a complement to long-context capacity, not solely a remedy for limited input length. It targets answer contexts that retain supporting evidence while concentrating on the query, using a reusable semantic hierarchy to guide source-preserving selection. Appendix A.1 provides a detailed comparison with evaluated baselines and selected related methods.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview
sections.text: Given a document D D and query q q , TreeFuse constructs an answer context C ⁡ ( q , D ) C(q,D) by selecting source-grounded semantic units. The objective is to retain supporting information while limiting content unrelated to the query, even when the full document fits within the model’s context window. Source selection does not create new source evidence; it changes which content is visible to the answer model and how that content is organized. TreeFuse therefore separates the information used to select evidence from the text delivered for answering. A compact semantic view exposes a node’s topic and structural role, while its original text retains details not captured by the description. Selecting complete local units preserves the surroundings of a match, and ancestor completion retains structural connections without including every neighboring branch. TreeFuse combines a reusable hierarchy with query-dependent selection and pruning. Figure 2 outlines the pipeline. First, source-grounded semantic tree construction links node descriptions and hierarchical relations to original source spans (§ 3.2 ). Given a query, structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate nodes from this shared representation (§ 3.3 ). Their union is completed with ancestor nodes and used to prune the original tree, yielding an answer context that preserves retained structural relations and complete local source text (§ 3.4 ). Figure 2: Overview of TreeFuse. (a) A single generation constructs a semantic hierarchy whose nodes are aligned to original source spans. (b) Structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution independently nominate nodes from this shared representation. (c) Their union is completed with ancestor nodes and used to prune the original tree. Retained nodes preserve their structural relations and complete local source text for answering.

sections.heading: 3.2 Source-Grounded Semantic Tree Construction
sections.text: The document-to-hierarchy mapping in Figure 2 links document structure to original source text. A pretrained language model receives the full document and jointly proposes semantic boundaries and parent–child relations in one main generation. Its output contains an ordered hierarchy, node titles, summaries, atomic facts, and verbatim boundary clues. A source-alignment procedure resolves these clues to document offsets, yielding a hierarchy T ⁡ ( D ) = ( V , E ) T(D)=(V,E) . Each node owns a local source span rather than the concatenation of its descendants. Its identity links the semantic view, source interval, and position in the hierarchy, so semantic scoring and lexical matching can nominate the same underlying source unit. The descriptions provide an indexing view; the original spans provide answer evidence. This source-grounded hierarchy is constructed independently of queries and can be reused across queries and answer models. Construction prompts, source alignment, and a case illustrating the tree’s utility for downstream QA appear in Appendices A.2 , A.3 , and E.5 , respectively.

sections.heading: 3.3 Query-Adaptive Dual-Granularity Selection
sections.text: The two channels in the dual-granularity selection module of Figure 2 nominate nodes from the shared hierarchy using complementary views. Structural–semantic scoring assesses a node’s relevance and supporting role from its descriptions and structural context. Fine-grained lexical attribution identifies localized matches in its original text, including entities, values, or phrases not captured by the descriptions. The channels produce node sets independently rather than averaging scores with different scales and meanings. Their selections may overlap: a node can be nominated by either channel or both.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: For source-grounded tree construction (§ 3.2 ) , we use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B \citep qwen36modelcard2026 to generate the semantic hierarchy and node descriptions, and a forward source matcher to align generated boundary clues with original document spans. The resulting trees are cached for reuse. For dual-granularity node selection (§ 3.3 ) , the semantic channel uses the same Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model to score nodes against the query, while the lexical channel uses node-level BM25 scores obtained by taking the maximum normalized score over each node’s source-text subunits. For structure-preserving pruning (§ 3.4 ) , we take the union of the two selections, add ancestor nodes, and prune unselected branches while preserving parent–child links and complete local source text. LongBench receives the resulting tree-structured JSON; LaRA formats the retained nodes as numbered source chunks with ancestor-title provenance. We evaluate these contexts with Qwen3.8-Max \citep qwen38max2026, DeepSeek-V4-Pro \citep deepseekv4doc2026, Kimi-K2.6 \citep kimik26blog2026, and GLM-5.3 \citep glm53docs2026, reusing each query’s constructed context across answer models without model-specific fine-tuning and holding it fixed across three answer-generation runs. sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate context construction across complementary QA settings and document domains, with four frontier answer models testing the reuse of the same selected contexts. Following prior compression research \citep longllmlingua2024, LongBench \citep longbench2024 provides scientific-document QA through Qasper \citep dasigi2021qasper and multi-passage reasoning through HotpotQA \citep yang2018hotpotqa and 2WikiMultihopQA \citep ho2020twowiki. We follow its official answer templates and normalized token-overlap QA-F1 scoring. LaRA-32K \citep lara2025 complements these tasks with 887 questions spanning 64 books, scientific papers, and financial reports, testing transfer across document domains. We report accuracy using LaRA’s official task-specific grading prompts with a fixed gpt-oss-20b judge. All methods and answer models share the same question set per dataset across three runs. Scores average the runs; Overall equally averages the four model scores on this common set. The LongBench summary weights its three tasks equally. Context reduction compares mean answer-context character counts with Raw on aligned examples. Sample alignment is detailed in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Raw context passes the uncompressed context and question to the answer model. Baselines include LongLLMLingua \citep longllmlingua2024 ( LongLL ) for query-aware token compression; Provence \citep provence2025 for sentence pruning; HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 for hierarchical chunking and retrieval; BRIEF-Pro \citep briefpro2026 for generative compression; and adapted LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 for query-aware document refinement. We use reported construction settings where applicable. To compare performance at similar mean context lengths, we also adjust baseline budgets or pruning thresholds toward TreeFuse ’s retained length, reporting achieved lengths and scores. See Appendices B.3 and C.3 for details.

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 summarize the LongBench and LaRA comparisons under the evaluation protocol in § 4.1 . We examine answering performance across tasks and answer models, followed by an analysis of the evidence retained in the constructed contexts. Run-level confidence intervals are reported in Appendix C.1 . Compression–performance analysis and comparisons at adjusted context lengths are provided in Appendices C.2 and C.3 .

sections.heading: Higher average QA-F1 with shorter answer contexts.
sections.text: TreeFuse achieves the highest four-model average QA-F1 among the evaluated methods on each of the three LongBench tasks. Across tasks, it improves over Raw by 1.72 QA-F1 points while reducing answer-context length by 58.55% . The gains are larger on the two multi-hop tasks: TreeFuse reaches Overall scores of 71.23 on HotpotQA and 73.09 on 2WikiMQA, exceeding Raw by 1.72 and 2.46 points, respectively. On 2WikiMQA with Kimi-K2.6, the score rises from 47.44 to 54.44—a 7.00-point absolute improvement and a 14.76% relative gain . The larger gains on tasks requiring information integration across passages are consistent with the motivation for structure-conditioned selection. These results directly address our research question: even when the complete document is available to the answer model, selecting and organizing its content can improve average answering performance rather than merely reduce input length. Appendix C.4 quantifies when answer-input savings offset amortized tree construction and query selection under model-weighted input-token accounting.

sections.heading: Gains across answer models with shared contexts.
sections.text: TreeFuse improves the LongBench average for every evaluated answer model , despite all four backbones already offering strong long-context capabilities. The largest gain occurs on Kimi-K2.6, whose average rises from 52.42 to 56.19—an absolute improvement of 3.77 points and a relative gain of 7.19%. Qwen3.8-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.3 improve by 1.48, 0.44, and 1.20 points, respectively. This consistency across model families suggests that the method is not tied to a particular backbone. These gains require no answer-model-specific context construction or fine-tuning : the same prepared contexts are reused across models. They show that access to the full document does not eliminate the value of upstream information organization and selection. Table 2: LaRA accuracy (%) averaged over three answer runs. sections.heading: Cross-benchmark performance.
sections.text: LaRA extends the evaluation to heterogeneous document domains and question types. Under the main-comparison settings in Table 2 , all evaluated external baselines exhibit substantial declines in four-model average accuracy relative to Raw, ranging from 6.21 to 39.27 points. In contrast, TreeFuse achieves the highest four-model average accuracy with 43.87% less answer context , increasing accuracy from 80.17 to 80.59. DeepSeek-V4-Pro gains 1.62 accuracy points over Raw. This contrast shows that substantial context reduction need not come at the expense of average answer quality in this setting. Together with the LongBench results, it supports the applicability of source-grounded context construction across different long-document evaluation settings.

TreeFuse achieves the highest Overall on all three datasets, together with the highest ECP on Qasper (52.95) and 2WikiMQA (62.01) and the second-highest on HotpotQA (42.11). The component scores clarify these ECP results. On Qasper, TreeFuse preserves nearly the same complete-evidence coverage as HiChunk (96.57% versus 96.00%) while achieving higher purity (9.33% versus 5.80%). On 2WikiMQA, TreeFuse combines the second-highest All-hit and purity to attain the highest ECP. These comparisons characterize a combination of support retention and concentration, rather than dominance in either component alone. This pattern is consistent with the design of selecting structurally relevant source nodes and supplementing them with precise lexical matches while preserving the local context of retained evidence.

sections.heading: Semantic and lexical selection.
sections.text: We test whether the two selection channels contribute beyond increasing context length by comparing three variants in Table 4 . Semantic-only retains semantic selections and their ancestor context, removing lexical supplementation. Lexical-only (BM) uses lexical node selection with ancestor closure under an approximately matched character budget. Semantic-only (BM) instead supplements semantic selections with random nodes using a single fixed seed, approaching the full method’s context length without targeted lexical matching. TreeFuse reaches 81.12 average QA-F1 , exceeding Semantic-only by 0.84 points, Lexical-only (BM) by 6.16 points, and Semantic-only (BM) by 2.72 points. The smaller difference from Semantic-only indicates that semantic selection accounts for most of the observed performance, with lexical matching providing an incremental contribution. On HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA, the full method exceeds Semantic-only by 0.81 and 0.88 points, whereas random supplementation scores 1.66 and 2.10 points lower than Semantic-only. These contrasts favor targeted supplementation over the tested random-expansion configuration , rather than attributing the improvement simply to additional context. To examine whether these performance differences are accompanied by differences in evidence retention, we match each variant’s saved context against the mapped gold annotations used in our source-evidence analysis (Appendix D.1 ). Span Recall measures length-weighted coverage of annotated source evidence. Table 16 in Appendix E.3 reports the conditional results. Its pooled column shows that, on the annotated subsets across all three tasks, including Qasper, TreeFuse has 21.50 percentage points higher Span Recall and 4.45 points higher QA-F1 than Lexical-only (BM), pooling over questions. Relative to the original Semantic-only configuration, the corresponding differences are 1.17 percentage points and 0.36 QA-F1. These contrasts are consistent with structural–semantic selection providing most evidence coverage and lexical matching serving as a smaller, targeted supplement. The HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA columns of Table 16 also show that the full method obtains 2.42 and 2.76 points higher QA-F1 than Semantic-only (BM) on their annotated subsets, despite small differences in aggregate Span Recall. sections.text: We ask how joint tree construction compares with staged and adapted representations . Table 6 compares these strategies under the same downstream selection framework. Within the tested selector, Qwen3.8-Max answer model, and two multi-hop tasks, the single-pass constructor achieves 81.12 average QA-F1 , compared with 78.90 for Multi-stage and 78.34 for the HiChunk adapter. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We revisited retrieval in the long-context era as a problem of selecting and organizing evidence, rather than merely fitting documents into a limited window. TreeFuse operationalizes this view through a training-free, reusable semantic hierarchy: abstraction guides selection, while structure-preserving pruning retains original text for answering. Across four frontier answer models, TreeFuse improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks with 58.55% less answer context, and achieves the highest four-model average accuracy on LaRA with 43.87% less context. Under the main evaluation settings, all compared retrieval and compression baselines fall below Raw in four-model average performance on each LongBench task and LaRA, whereas TreeFuse exceeds it. This contrast validates the value of adaptive context construction while showing that input reduction alone does not ensure better answers. The central design principle is to use abstraction to decide what to retain without substituting it for the source evidence. Long-context capacity and retrieval thus address complementary decisions: how much information can be made available, and which source content and relations should be presented for a particular question. Our findings establish the latter as a consequential design choice even when the former no longer prevents full-document input.

sections.heading: Limitation and Future Work.
sections.text: Our evaluation centers on long-document question answering. Extending TreeFuse to multimodal documents would require linking textual evidence with tables and figures. Although retained text is source-grounded, selection still depends on generated structure and descriptions. Controlled perturbation studies could quantify this sensitivity and guide more robust tree construction and selection. Future work could also explore other evidence-intensive tasks and incremental tree updates as documents evolve, extending the reusable hierarchy beyond the settings evaluated here.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with writing, specifically for language polishing, grammar correction, and improving the clarity of exposition in text that was first drafted by the authors. We also used generative AI tools as coding assistants for routine, non-novel implementation tasks (e.g., boilerplate code, plotting scripts, and refactoring). We have not used generative AI tools to generate research ideas, formulate the core hypotheses, design the method, produce or analyze experimental results, or draw scientific conclusions; these were carried out entirely by the authors.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: TreeFuse uses public benchmarks and involves no human-subject studies or collection of new personal data. Dataset and model use follows their respective terms. Source-preserving selection does not guarantee factual correctness or privacy protection; sensitive applications require appropriate safeguards.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: Our code is available through the code repository linked in the paper. The appendices document prompts, selection rules, experimental settings, and evaluation procedures. Fixed contexts are reused across answer models and repeated runs; API updates and stochastic generation may affect exact replication.

sections.text: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B proposes section paths, titles, summaries, atomic facts, and verbatim boundary clues. Parent paths define the hierarchy without duplicating child text inside parent nodes.

sections.heading: Semantic cutoff.
sections.text: Node ratings lie in [ 0 , 10 ] [0,10] . The selector requests three cutoff suggestions and uses the minimum valid value in [ 1 , 10 ] [1,10] . It lowers this cutoff as needed to approach the coverage floor, including ancestor context. Default floors are 2% of source characters and three nodes, increasing to 5% and five nodes for detected location questions. A fallback handles missing cutoff responses, and an empty selection is replaced by the highest-scoring root and its subtree.

sections.heading: Lexical cutoff.
sections.text: BM25 is computed over a shared pool of source-text subunits. Short fragments below 40 characters are merged into their preceding unit when one exists. For nonconstant scores, normalization is z u = ( b u − b min ) / ( b max − b min ) z_{u}=(b_{u}-b_{\min})/(b_{\max}-b_{\min}) over the complete document pool. Node scores are the maxima of their subunit scores, with zero assigned to a node without subunits. For every dataset, the lexical cutoff is the 90th percentile (P90) of the node-score distribution. The percentile uses linear interpolation and includes ties, so it does not select exactly 10% of nodes. Ancestor closure can further enlarge the set.

sections.text: The break-even thresholds are 5.40–6.83 on HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA, 10.24–10.64 on Qasper, and 1.66–1.82 on LaRA. sections.heading: D.1 Evidence Annotations and Source Alignment
sections.text: Qasper uses mapped textual evidence with alternative annotation sets. HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA use mapped supporting passages. The component results are reported in Table 3 ; the metrics quantify annotated source preservation rather than semantic answer sufficiency.

sections.heading: Complete evidence coverage.
sections.text: Let 𝒢 i \mathcal{G}_{i} contain the eligible evidence sets for question i i and r ⁡ ( u , C i ) r(u,C_{i}) denote normalized literal coverage of evidence unit u u in context C i C_{i} . The matcher checks normalized source text and sentence or line segments. We define A i = [ ∃ G ∈ 𝒢 i : r ( u , C i ) ≥ 0.999 for every u ∈ G ] , All - hit = 100 N ∑ i = 1 N A i . A_{i}=\mathbb{1}\!\left[\exists G\in\mathcal{G}_{i}:r(u,C_{i})\geq 0.999\ \text{for every }u\in G\right],\qquad\mathrm{All\text{-}hit}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}A_{i}. (6) Thus, one completely covered alternative is sufficient. Passage-level All-hit measures literal preservation, not the validity of a reasoning chain or semantic answer sufficiency.

sections.heading: Evidence concentration.
sections.text: For purity, selected content is aligned to normalized lexical tokens in the original document. Let P i P_{i} be the set of distinct recovered source-token positions, G i ∗ G_{i}^{*} the mapped reference-token set, and U i U_{i} the number of unmapped output tokens after method-specific content extraction. Then Evidence ​ Purity = 100 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N | P i ∩ G i ∗ | max ⁡ ( 1 , | P i | + U i ) . \mathrm{Evidence\ Purity}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|P_{i}\cap G_{i}^{*}|}{\max(1,|P_{i}|+U_{i})}. (7) For Qasper, eligible textual alternatives must map to source tokens, and the scorer chooses the alternative with greatest token recall, breaking ties by source-token intersection-over-union. This rule differs from the literal complete-coverage test used for All-hit. For the multi-hop tasks, reference positions are obtained from the mapped supporting-passage spans. Whole units are matched first, with line-level fallback. Token-pruned outputs use sequence alignment. Structural wrappers are excluded where the parser extracts source content. Recovered source positions are deduplicated, so the denominator is not a literal count of every token sent to the answer model. Unmapped text can include valid paraphrases, and unannotated context can still support answering. Purity is consequently an annotation-based concentration proxy rather than the fraction of all useful information in the output.

sections.heading: D.3 Equal-Weight ECP Rationale
sections.text: To summarize completeness and concentration without introducing a tunable trade-off, we use their equal-weight arithmetic mean: ECP = 1 2 ​ ( All ​ - ​ hit + Evidence ​ Purity ) . \mathrm{ECP}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{All\text{-}hit}+\mathrm{Evidence\ Purity}\right). (8) All-hit measures whether a complete annotated evidence set is retained, whereas Evidence Purity measures how concentrated the selected content is around mapped evidence. Equal weighting treats these as complementary diagnostic dimensions and avoids choosing a dataset-dependent preference between completeness and concentration. Because both components are percentages, ECP remains on the same 0 0 – 100 100 scale. The same aggregation is applied to every method and dataset; it is a source-evidence diagnostic rather than a model of answer correctness.

sections.text: Table 6 compares representations supplied to the same downstream selection framework. The single-pass and multi-stage constructors both use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Single-pass construction generates the hierarchy and node descriptions jointly from the document, as described in Appendix A.3 . It denotes a joint generation design, not a guarantee of exactly one request when output validation requires a retry.

sections.heading: Multi-stage construction.
sections.text: The alternative pipeline separates structure extraction, source anchoring, and content enrichment. It first partitions the source into indexed chunks with an 800-token target while respecting passage boundaries, then forms groups of up to 20,000 tokens with one-chunk overlap. An initial call proposes an outline containing titles, hierarchy paths, and chunk indices. Subsequent groups extend the existing outline, with an additional repair step for uncovered chunks when needed. A combined validation and localization stage checks candidate headings against their source chunks and identifies section boundaries. These anchors are mapped to document character positions to assemble the tree and attach local source text. Oversized leaf nodes can be subdivided before bottom-up content enrichment. Leaf descriptions use their own text, whereas internal-node descriptions combine local introductory text with child summaries. The pipeline receives the complete document, but individual calls operate on groups, chunks, or node material. The initial outline call can see the full document when it fits within one group.

sections.heading: Configuration and downstream selection.
sections.text: Validation and localization batch up to five chunks per call. Leaf subdivision uses a 16,000-token threshold and a recursion-depth limit of two. Content enrichment produces summaries and facts, batching up to six nodes with 16,000 characters of material per batch and an 8,000-character per-node limit. Both representations feed the semantic scorer, adaptive cutoff, ancestor completion, and lexical-union procedure. The selector uses the P90 lexical cutoff on both HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA. Node boundaries, metadata, and the selected content can therefore differ despite the shared selection framework.

sections.heading: HiChunk representation adapter.
sections.text: This configuration adapts cached HiChunk-derived segments and hierarchy levels to the common representation interface required by our downstream selector. The adaptation is introduced only for compatibility with the shared selection framework used in this comparison. It therefore evaluates a HiChunk-derived representation with our downstream selection procedure, rather than the complete HiChunk retrieval and Auto-Merge system.

sections.heading: Lexical supplementation: recovering data provenance.
sections.text: A Qasper question asks, “How is the dataset of hashtags sourced?” The source identifies “1,268 randomly selected tweets in the Stanford Sentiment Analysis Dataset” and “all 12,594 unique English hashtags and their associated tweets from the same Stanford dataset.” Compared with Semantic-only (BM), Full raises Span Recall from 0 to 100 and mean QA-F1 from 0 to 71.11. This illustrates the value of retaining source-specific provenance in the selected context.

sections.heading: Semantic support: connecting a mission to its destination.
sections.text: A HotpotQA question asks, “Gary L. Bennett was a part of the space missions that have a primary destination of what celestial body?” The source links Bennett to the Ulysses mission and states that Ulysses “was a robotic space probe whose primary mission was to orbit the Sun and study it at all latitudes.” Compared with Lexical-only (BM), Full raises Span Recall from 2.10 to 82.89. All three lexical-only answers name Jupiter, whereas all three Full answers name the Sun, changing mean QA-F1 from 0 to 100. The example illustrates how the selected source context can connect a named participant to the mission target.

sections.heading: Evidence enrichment without an answer-score change.
sections.text: Another HotpotQA question asks, “Which California band, whose debut album Adrenaline appeared in 1995, has been referred to as ‘the Radiohead of metal’?” The source identifies Deftones and states, “The band’s experimental nature has led some critics to describe them as ẗhe Radiohead of metal.̈” lexical-only (BM) and Full both answer Deftones in all three runs. Full increases Span Recall from 87.28 to 96.34 while mean QA-F1 remains 100. Thus, identical correct answers can arise from contexts with different annotated-evidence coverage. These are examples from the recorded configurations described in Appendix B.2 , not isolated causal tests.

sections.heading: Routing metadata and source evidence.
sections.text: Generated boundaries, hierarchy, summaries, and facts can affect which source regions are selected. The relevant distinction is between evidence containment and exact recovery of annotation boundaries: the tree organizes source regions for retrieval rather than reproducing a unique gold segmentation. Titles and structural paths provide navigation, while summaries and facts guide selection rather than substitute for source evidence in the answer context. The source matcher anchors nodes to document text; when both summary and facts are absent, scoring uses a source-text prefix (Appendix A.3 ). The following case examines whether a node broader than individual evidence units can still retain their support.

sections.heading: A coherent region containing the annotated mechanism.
sections.text: The Qasper example qasper-125-5724368043143d51-q151 asks, “How are weights dynamically adjusted?” One annotated alternative evidence set contains four units, all mapped to node n8 . These units explain why easy-negative examples dominate training, the modification that multiplies soft probability p p by ( 1 − p ) (1-p) , how this factor changes during training to down-weight easy examples, and its connection to focal loss. The node contains the mechanism together with its motivation and interpretation, rather than assigning a separate annotation-aligned boundary to each unit. The four-unit set is the alternative used for the case metrics below, not the union of all annotations for this question; matching follows Appendices D.1 and D.2 .

sections.heading: Implication for construction reliability.
sections.text: This case establishes a narrower requirement than boundary-perfect reconstruction: a coherent source node can preserve the required evidence without matching its annotation boundaries . For source-grounded selection to work, the relevant text must remain represented in selectable nodes, those nodes must be retrieved, and their original text must reach the reader. Boundary or metadata differences need not remove support when these conditions remain satisfied. Conversely, source grounding does not prevent incorrect metadata or structure from causing a selection miss. This is an observed containment case, not a controlled corruption experiment or an estimate of tree-construction error rates. It supports separating routing metadata from answer evidence, rather than treating arbitrary construction errors as harmless.

Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Tianhao Liao Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Zhenqing Ling Affiliation: Alibaba Group Ying Shen Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Yaliang Li Affiliation: Alibaba Group Daoyuan Chen Affiliation: Alibaba Group Abstract Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce TreeFuse , a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. TreeFuse constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, TreeFuse improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55%. Our code is available at the code repository . 1 Introduction Frontier language models can increasingly accommodate entire documents within their context windows, making full-context prompting a practical option for long-document question answering. Yet input capacity and context selection address different questions: how much information a model can receive, and which information it should receive for a particular query. Prior work shows that performance can depend strongly on where relevant information appears within a long context, even when that information remains available to the model \citep liu2024lost. Prior compression methods show that selecting context can improve answering as well as shorten the input \citep longllmlingua2024,provence2025, while LaRA \citep lara2025 finds no universally preferable choice between retrieval-based and full-context approaches. These findings motivate rethinking retrieval beyond accommodating input-length constraints: When the full document already fits within the context window, can retrieval improve answering, and how should it select the supporting context? A relevant passage is not always sufficient to support an answer. A question may require a directly mentioned fact together with background or a relation established elsewhere in the document. Sufficient Context \citep joren2025sufficient explicitly distinguishes contextual support from answer correctness. Context construction must therefore consider both the support it retains and how selectively it presents that support. Narrow extraction can omit a necessary fact or separate a detail from its interpretation, whereas broad expansion may introduce unrelated material. Controlled studies of arithmetic reasoning show that such irrelevant information can interfere with model predictions \citep shi2023distracted, motivating attention to context concentration as well as support retention. Hierarchical methods such as HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 make document organization available to retrieval and refinement. The remaining design question is how to use that organization while remaining sensitive to precise source-level details. Figure 1: A schematic example contrasts full context with distractors, incomplete retrieval with missing support, and TreeFuse ’s focused context retaining both supporting statements. To reconcile support retention with context concentration, we separate the information used to select evidence from the text supplied for answering. Figure 1 illustrates the goal: retaining supporting facts and their relation while excluding unrelated material. We instantiate this principle with TreeFuse , a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while preserving original evidence. Step 1: Source-grounded Semantic Tree Construction. A pretrained model jointly proposes semantic boundaries and hierarchical relations from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to original source spans. The resulting hierarchy is query-independent and reusable. Step 2: Query-adaptive Context Construction. Structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate nodes from this shared representation. A localized lexical match can retain a complete source node, supplementing semantic judgments with precise details. The selected nodes and their ancestors form a pruned hierarchy that preserves the original parent–child relations and complete local text. The same constructed context can be supplied to different answer models without model-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate TreeFuse with four frontier answer models that offer strong long-context processing capabilities: Qwen3.8-Max \citep qwen38max2026, DeepSeek-V4-Pro \citep deepseekv4doc2026, Kimi-K2.6 \citep kimik26blog2026, and GLM-5.3 \citep glm53docs2026. Full-context prompting provides a direct reference for testing whether retrieval remains beneficial when the complete document is already available to the answer model. Across three LongBench QA tasks, TreeFuse reduces the answer-context length by 58.55% on average while improving the four-model average by 1.72 QA-F1 points over full-context prompting. The gains are more pronounced on the multi-hop HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA tasks, where the four-model averages improve by 1.72 and 2.46 points, respectively. On 2WikiMQA with Kimi-K2.6, TreeFuse achieves a 7.00-point improvement, corresponding to a 14.76% relative gain. Evaluation on LaRA further tests transfer across heterogeneous long-document tasks, where TreeFuse achieves the highest four-model average accuracy among the evaluated methods with 43.87% less answer context. Beyond answer scores, source-evidence analyses examine completeness and concentration, while component comparisons characterize semantic and lexical selection, hierarchical organization, and single-pass construction. These evaluations address both parts of our research question, establishing average gains over full-context prompting and examining how the selected contexts retain and organize supporting evidence. To summarize, our contributions are: • We empirically demonstrate that query-adaptive context construction can improve average answering performance even when full-document input is feasible, positioning retrieval as a complement to long-context capacity. • We introduce reusable semantic trees and dual-granularity selection to coordinate structural support with precise source details, retaining complete local text without method-specific training. • We provide a broad evaluation across four frontier answer-model families and diverse long-document tasks, obtaining a 1.72-point average QA-F1 improvement on the three LongBench tasks with 58.55% less context. We release our code to support research on adaptive context construction: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE . 2 Related Work Retrieval and Compression for Long-Context Question Answering LongBench \citep longbench2024 and LaRA \citep lara2025 evaluate long-context understanding and retrieval-based answering. LongRAG by \citet jiang2024longrag groups related documents into larger retrieval units to exploit long-context models. A separate LongRAG by \citet zhao2024longrag jointly addresses global information and factual details in long-context QA. Compression methods act at different granularities: LongLLMLingua \citep longllmlingua2024 prunes tokens, Provence \citep provence2025 selects sentences, and RECOMP \citep recomp2024 and BRIEF-Pro \citep briefpro2026 learn or generate compact contexts. ACC-RAG \citep accrag2025 adapts compression rates, while SARA \citep sara2025 combines textual and compressed representations. Sufficient Context \citep joren2025sufficient examines whether supplied information is sufficient for answering. Semantic Chunking and Hierarchical Document Indexing Semantic chunkers such as LumberChunker \citep lumberchunker2024 and Meta-Chunking \citep metachunking2025 seek coherent boundaries, with libraries such as Chonkie 1 1 1 https://docs.chonkie.ai/ providing multiple implementations. Hierarchical indexes additionally organize relationships among units. RAPTOR \citep raptor2024 recursively clusters and summarizes passages. TreeRAG \citep tao2025treerag combines tree-based chunking with bidirectional traversal. SiReRAG \citep zhang2025sirerag constructs similarity and relatedness trees and combines their nodes in a retrieval pool. Heading-aware indexing \citep headingaware2025 exploits existing sections, while HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 learn specialized components for hierarchical chunking or refinement. Structure-Aware and Hybrid Retrieval BM25 \citep robertson2009bm25 and DPR \citep karpukhin2020dpr provide lexical and learned semantic relevance signals. Contextual Retrieval \citep anthropic2024contextual prepends explanatory context to chunks before embedding and BM25 indexing. MemWalker \citep chen2023memwalker interactively navigates summary trees, while PageIndex \citep pageindex2025 uses reasoning-based search over document hierarchies. HiChunk \citep hichunk2025 expands retrieval hits through Auto-Merge, and LongRefiner \citep longrefiner2025 performs query-aware refinement. DISRetrieval \citep chen2026disretrieval combines discourse parsing, LLM-enhanced node representations, and structure-guided hierarchical retrieval. TreeFuse approaches retrieval as a complement to long-context capacity, not solely a remedy for limited input length. It targets answer contexts that retain supporting evidence while concentrating on the query, using a reusable semantic hierarchy to guide source-preserving selection. Appendix A.1 provides a detailed comparison with evaluated baselines and selected related methods. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview Given a document D D and query q q , TreeFuse constructs an answer context C ⁡ ( q , D ) C(q,D) by selecting source-grounded semantic units. The objective is to retain supporting information while limiting content unrelated to the query, even when the full document fits within the model’s context window. Source selection does not create new source evidence; it changes which content is visible to the answer model and how that content is organized. TreeFuse therefore separates the information used to select evidence from the text delivered for answering. A compact semantic view exposes a node’s topic and structural role, while its original text retains details not captured by the description. Selecting complete local units preserves the surroundings of a match, and ancestor completion retains structural connections without including every neighboring branch. TreeFuse combines a reusable hierarchy with query-dependent selection and pruning. Figure 2 outlines the pipeline. First, source-grounded semantic tree construction links node descriptions and hierarchical relations to original source spans (§ 3.2 ). Given a query, structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate nodes from this shared representation (§ 3.3 ). Their union is completed with ancestor nodes and used to prune the original tree, yielding an answer context that preserves retained structural relations and complete local source text (§ 3.4 ). Figure 2: Overview of TreeFuse. (a) A single generation constructs a semantic hierarchy whose nodes are aligned to original source spans. (b) Structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution independently nominate nodes from this shared representation. (c) Their union is completed with ancestor nodes and used to prune the original tree. Retained nodes preserve their structural relations and complete local source text for answering. 3.2 Source-Grounded Semantic Tree Construction The document-to-hierarchy mapping in Figure 2 links document structure to original source text. A pretrained language model receives the full document and jointly proposes semantic boundaries and parent–child relations in one main generation. Its output contains an ordered hierarchy, node titles, summaries, atomic facts, and verbatim boundary clues. A source-alignment procedure resolves these clues to document offsets, yielding a hierarchy T ⁡ ( D ) = ( V , E ) T(D)=(V,E) . Each node n i ∈ V n_{i}\in V has a semantic view m i m_{i} and a source view x i x_{i} : m i = ( p i , t i , s i , F i ) , x i = D [ a i : e i ] , m_{i}=(p_{i},t_{i},s_{i},F_{i}),\qquad x_{i}=D[a_{i}:e_{i}], (1) where p i p_{i} is its structural path, t i t_{i} its title, s i s_{i} its summary, F i F_{i} its atomic facts, and [ a i , e i ) [a_{i},e_{i}) its source interval. Each node owns a local source span rather than the concatenation of its descendants. Its identity links the semantic view, source interval, and position in the hierarchy, so semantic scoring and lexical matching can nominate the same underlying source unit. The descriptions provide an indexing view; the original spans provide answer evidence. This source-grounded hierarchy is constructed independently of queries and can be reused across queries and answer models. Construction prompts, source alignment, and a case illustrating the tree’s utility for downstream QA appear in Appendices A.2 , A.3 , and E.5 , respectively. 3.3 Query-Adaptive Dual-Granularity Selection The two channels in the dual-granularity selection module of Figure 2 nominate nodes from the shared hierarchy using complementary views. Structural–semantic scoring assesses a node’s relevance and supporting role from its descriptions and structural context. Fine-grained lexical attribution identifies localized matches in its original text, including entities, values, or phrases not captured by the descriptions. The channels produce node sets independently rather than averaging scores with different scales and meanings. Their selections may overlap: a node can be nominated by either channel or both. Structural–semantic scoring. For each query, a pretrained model rates every node on a 0 0 – 10 10 relevance scale using its semantic view, available parent metadata, and document-level structural context. The prompt requests judgments of direct relevance and supporting relationships. All nodes are scored, so a child remains eligible even if its parent scores low. The initial selection is R sem 0 ​ ( q ) = { n i ∈ V : r i sem ​ ( q ) ≥ τ ⁡ ( q , T ) } , R_{\mathrm{sem}}^{0}(q)=\{n_{i}\in V:r_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}(q)\geq\tau(q,T)\}, where r i sem ​ ( q ) r_{i}^{\mathrm{sem}}(q) is the node’s relevance rating and τ ⁡ ( q , T ) \tau(q,T) the semantic cutoff. Together with the hierarchy comparison in Table 5 , indicating that using document structure effectively does not require a more elaborate construction procedure. 5 Conclusion We revisited retrieval in the long-context era as a problem of selecting and organizing evidence, rather than merely fitting documents into a limited window. TreeFuse operationalizes this view through a training-free, reusable semantic hierarchy: abstraction guides selection, while structure-preserving pruning retains original text for answering. Across four frontier answer models, TreeFuse improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks with 58.55% less answer context, and achieves the highest four-model average accuracy on LaRA with 43.87% less context. Under the main evaluation settings, all compared retrieval and compression baselines fall below Raw in four-model average performance on each LongBench task and LaRA, whereas TreeFuse exceeds it. This contrast validates the value of adaptive context construction while showing that input reduction alone does not ensure better answers. The central design principle is to use abstraction to decide what to retain without substituting it for the source evidence. Long-context capacity and retrieval thus address complementary decisions: how much information can be made available, and which source content and relations should be presented for a particular question. Our findings establish the latter as a consequential design choice even when the former no longer prevents full-document input. Limitation and Future Work. Our evaluation centers on long-document question answering. Extending TreeFuse to multimodal documents would require linking textual evidence with tables and figures. Although retained text is source-grounded, selection still depends on generated structure and descriptions. Controlled perturbation studies could quantify this sensitivity and guide more robust tree construction and selection. Future work could also explore other evidence-intensive tasks and incremental tree updates as documents evolve, extending the reusable hierarchy beyond the settings evaluated here.
